messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 33
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Graphic Designer
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 34

She first noticed him because he was always there. Not in a way she could prove at first—just a shape at the edge of her peripheral vision, a figure who seemed to be walking the same route home from the train station, browsing the same grocery aisles, sitting two tables away at the café she liked. She told herself it was coincidence. She was a graphic designer, trained to notice patterns, and she knew that the mind often creates meaning where none exists. So she dismissed it.

But then the notes began. Small, folded pieces of paper tucked under her windshield wiper: *You look prettiest when you’re focused.* She had been hunched over her laptop at a coffee shop the day before, working on a branding project for a local bakery. When she saw the note, her stomach dropped. She looked around the parking lot. No one. The next day, another note: *Your hair smells like rain.* She had been caught in the rain on Tuesday. That afternoon she told her husband, Mark, and they went to the police. There was nothing they could do yet, the officer explained—no direct threat, no physical harm. She should document everything, keep a log.

Over the next few weeks, she stopped going to the coffee shop. She took different routes home, sometimes driving an extra fifteen minutes just to lose him. She changed her routine at work, leaving at odd hours, her eyes scanning the sidewalk before she stepped out. Mark started picking her up when he could, but he couldn’t be there all the time. The notes kept coming. Once, she found one taped to her studio door: *I know when you’re alone.* That was the night she couldn’t stop shaking. She barely slept.

Now, months later, he has been arrested and charged. The trial is pending. She knows she is safe—she moved offices, changed her phone number, installed cameras at home—but her body doesn’t believe it. She still checks her rearview mirror compulsively, her hands sweating on the wheel. She walks through the grocery store with her head on a swivel, heart hammering every time a man of average height with brown hair turns down an aisle. She no longer works in coffee shops; she works from home, curtains drawn, jumping at every sound. Her design work suffers. She stares at the screen for hours, unable to choose a font, unable to commit to a color palette because her mind is stuck in a loop: *He knew I was working there. He knew what I smelled like. What else does he know?*

She avoids crowds. She avoids the train station. She avoids the email notifications she used to ignore, now checking each one twice before opening. Her husband tries to comfort her, but she feels distant from him, hollowed out. She snaps at him for little things—leaving the back door unlocked, telling a neighbor about their new security system. She doesn’t trust anyone anymore, not even her closest friends. She canceled a coffee date last week because she saw a man in a blue jacket that looked like the one he always wore.

At night, she dreams of notes. Hundreds of them, piling up on her desk, her bed, her keyboard. She wakes up gasping, her skin crawling. She tells herself it’s over. But her body remembers.
